turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’m here for a routine checkup, but I’ve noticed a lesion on my scalp. I don’t have any other symptoms and I feel generally well.
How long have you noticed this lesion on your scalp, and has it changed in size, color, or appearance since you first noticed it?

Patient: I noticed the scalp lesion a few months ago, and I think it’s slowly grown a bit. The color and shape have changed slightly since I first saw it, but I haven’t had any pain or other symptoms.
Can you describe the appearance of the lesion in more detail? Specifically, what color is it, and does it have a scaly, crusty, smooth, or pearly surface texture?

Patient: It’s on the top of my scalp, kind of reddish-brown, with a scaly surface that sometimes looks a little crusted. It doesn’t feel painful, and the center seems a bit more rough than the surrounding skin.
Has the lesion ever bled, ulcerated, or developed a sore that doesn't heal?

Patient: I haven’t noticed it bleeding or becoming ulcerated, and it hasn’t developed an open sore that won’t heal. It’s mainly been slowly changing with that scaly, slightly crusted surface, but it still isn’t painful.
Do you have a history of significant sun exposure, sunburns, or do you spend considerable time outdoors without scalp protection (like a hat)?

Yes—I'm outside a lot for jogging and gardening, and I usually don’t wear a hat; I’ve had some sun exposure and occasional sunburns over the years. I first noticed it a few months ago on the top of my scalp, and it’s been slowly changing with a scaly, slightly crusted look.
Is the lesion raised or flat, and when you touch it, does it feel soft or firm/hard compared to the surrounding skin?
Patient: It seems a bit raised compared to the surrounding skin, and when I touch it, it feels firmer and harder than the nearby scalp, not soft. It doesn’t hurt when I press on it.

Is the lesion sharply defined with a distinct border, or does it blend gradually into the surrounding skin? And when you run your finger across it, does it feel like sandpaper or more like a solid bump?
Patient: It has a pretty distinct border, and it doesn’t blend much into the surrounding skin. When I run my finger across it, it feels rough—more like a sandpapery surface than just a smooth bump.
Are there any other similar scaly spots or patches on your scalp, face, or hands, or is this the only lesion you've noticed?
Patient: I haven’t noticed any other similar scaly spots or patches on my scalp, face, or hands—this is the only one.
What is the approximate size of the lesion (in millimeters or centimeters), and does it have a central indentation, keratin plug, or any hair loss within it?

Patient: It’s about 1 centimeter across, maybe a little bigger, and I don’t notice any hair loss directly on it. I haven’t seen a central indentation or a clear keratin plug, just a rough, scaly, slightly crusted center.

What is your age, and have you ever been told you have "sun spots" or precancerous lesions before, or do you have any condition that affects your immune system?

(If you prefer to proceed with the differential based on current information, I can do so, but age would help refine the pre-test probability significantly.)
Patient: I’m 68, and I haven’t been told I have any “sun spots” or precancerous lesions before. I also don’t have any immune system condition or take immune-suppressing medications.
[DDX] Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Bowen's Disease (Squamous Cell Carcinoma in situ), Hypertrophic Actinic Keratosis, Basal Cell Carcinoma, Amelanotic Melanoma
